Mobile County housing snapshot

Alabama's southwestern corner belongs to Mobile County, the state's third most populous, with 414,809 residents at the last full count. The city of Mobile is both seat and largest city. Coastline runs through the county, including Dauphin Island, Gaillard Island and Mon Louis Island, and it drives insurance costs, flood maps and house values.

The county has 163,750 households and 184,441 housing units, 11.2% of them vacant. Owners live in 64.6% of occupied homes, and 35.4% are rented. A good many sellers are landlords, and some rentals have unpaid tax behind them.

The county has nine cities: Bayou La Batre, Chickasaw, Citronelle, Creola, Mobile, Prichard, Saraland, Satsuma and Semmes. Dauphin Island and Mount Vernon are towns. Communities such as Theodore, Grand Bay, Tillmans Corner, Axis, Chunchula and Wilmer have no city government. A house in Saraland, one in Theodore and one on Dauphin Island all sit in one county, but the millage and school levy on each can differ, so confirm the taxing districts for your parcel before trusting an online estimate.

Who handles property tax

Assessment and collection both sit with the Mobile County Revenue Commission. Every Wednesday its offices close, which trips people up in late December when lines are longest.

On a home sale, the Revenue Commission deals with value and billing, while the probate office records the deed. Do not mix up the two.

Landlords who supply appliances or furnishings, and anyone running a business with equipment at a house, face a personal property rule too. List it after October 1 and by December 31 at the latest. A listing filed past the third Monday in January draws a 10% penalty plus fees.

Delinquency timeline

The tax falls due October 1 and is delinquent after December 31. The state timetable follows.

MonthStep in the state timetable
October 1Taxes due
January 1Taxes delinquent
FebruaryTurned over to probate court
MarchProbate court meets
AprilAdvertised for sale
MayTax sale

Anyone who knows a bill is unpaid has until the end of December to clear it before delinquency begins. Selling is easiest if you act ahead of January.

Water and storms

Winters are mild and the air is humid. A 2007 study found about 66.3 inches of rain a year in Mobile, the most of any city in the contiguous 48 states. Inspectors look for water first, so roofs, drainage, crawl spaces and flood zones weigh heavily on a sale.

Category 3 Frederic crossed Mobile on September 12, 1979. Ivan hit on September 16, 2004. On August 29, 2005, Katrina pushed an 11.45 foot surge through downtown and the Battleship Parkway. Sally, in 2020, was the first hurricane since Ivan to strike Alabama head on, and a Category 3 Zeta came a month afterward.

Houses in eastern Mobile that flooded during Katrina, and any with storm repairs left half done, tend to stall on the open market. A cash buyer accepts them as they are.

Appeals and closing

Put a valuation challenge in writing to the county Board of Equalization. Its ruling may be taken to circuit court within 30 days. Alabama Code 40-3-25 calls for notice to the board secretary and the circuit clerk and a bond, and an appeal can be dismissed if last year's tax was not paid before delinquency.

A title company or closing attorney generally takes any tax payoff out of the seller's proceeds at the table. The probate court records the deed, with a deed tax of $0.50 per $500 of value under Alabama Code 40-22-1.

  • Request the current balance before you list or take an offer.
  • Check the parcel for exemptions that need to be released or reclaimed.
  • Gather the paperwork for any inherited property, since the deed chain must be clean.
  • Find out how the title company would treat a lien from an earlier year.

Who sells here

The typical county seller has a storm-worn roof, an aging house or an estate to settle. Many live in Mobile's historic neighborhoods, such as Ashland Place, Oakleigh Garden, Old Dauphin Way and Spring Hill, where upkeep costs more. Some hold houses in areas storms have hit before. Others inherited property and cannot cover repairs and back tax together.

What a cash sale skips

Selling to a buyer with a mortgage puts the house through an appraisal, a lender inspection and often an insurance check. In a county this wet, those steps expose trouble, from a worn roof to a damp crawl space, and each can lead to repair demands or a price cut.

None of that applies to a cash sale. The buyer sees the house as it is and prices it accordingly. Owners up against a deadline, whether a May tax sale, a move or an estate to wrap up, benefit most.

Inherited and rental properties

Inherited houses are common here, and the tax account does not wait for the estate. If the property passed to several heirs, work out who is the owner of record and who has authority to sign before anything is listed. The title company will not close until the deed chain is clean, and an open question about an heir can add weeks.

For a rental, check whether personal property such as appliances or furnishings has been listed on time. A missed listing deadline carries a penalty, and that balance can show up on the payoff. Ask the Revenue Commission for the full picture, real and personal, so nothing surprises you at the closing table.

Where a tenant lives in the house, tell the tenant early and keep showings polite and scheduled. A cooperative tenant makes a quick sale far easier, and a cash buyer can often take a house with the lease in place.

Steps from first call to closing

Step one is learning the balance: call the Revenue Commission, on any day but Wednesday, and ask about the amount owed and any earlier open year. Step two is collecting the deed and estate papers. Step three is requesting a written cash offer and comparing what you would net once the tax is paid.

Step four is picking a closing date with room for the title search. The title company verifies ownership, requests the payoff, drafts the settlement statement and arranges recording. You sign once, the tax is paid out of the proceeds, and the remainder goes to you.

For a rental, put the leases in the folder and decide whether the tenants will stay. The buyer will ask before the offer is final.

Finally, keep the payoff letter, the settlement statement and the recorded deed together after closing. They are your proof that the tax account was cleared.

Frequently asked questions

When is Mobile County property tax due?

It is due October 1 and becomes delinquent after December 31, and the Mobile County Revenue Commission does the collecting.

Is the Mobile County Revenue Commission open on Wednesdays?

No. Every office closes on Wednesdays, so go on another weekday.

What happens if I do not pay Mobile County property tax?

The bill turns delinquent after December 31. Probate court gets it in February, notices run in April, and a tax sale happens in May.

How long do I have to appeal an assessment in Mobile County?

Start with a written appeal to the Board of Equalization. To take the board's decision to circuit court, you have 30 days under Alabama Code 40-3-25.

Can I sell a Mobile County house that has back property tax?

Yes. Proceeds at closing cover the back tax through the title company. Get the balance from the Revenue Commission before you start.

Baldwin County housing and growth

Baldwin County sits on the Gulf coast on the eastern side of Mobile Bay. Bay Minette is the county seat and Daphne is the largest city. The population was 231,767 in the 2020 census, up from 182,265 in 2010, and the 2025 estimate is 267,761. Of the 124,148 housing units counted in 2020, 25.0 percent were vacant.

Growth is uneven. The Foley subdivision went from 48,089 to 64,862 people between 2010 and 2020, and the Daphne subdivision, which includes Spanish Fort, went from 41,295 to 55,767. The Stockton area stayed nearly flat, at 3,804 and 3,745. Two houses in the same county can sit in very different markets, so look at numbers for your own part of the county and not the county average.

School zoning varies too. The county has three public school districts: Baldwin County, Gulf Shores City and Orange Beach City, the last formed in 2022. A house in Orange Beach and one in Bay Minette share a county but not a school system, and buyers ask about that.

Cities and towns in the county

Baldwin has nine cities and five towns. The cities are Bay Minette, Daphne, Fairhope, Foley, Gulf Shores, Loxley, Orange Beach, Robertsdale and Spanish Fort. The towns are Elberta, Magnolia Springs, Perdido Beach, Silverhill and Summerdale. Point Clear, Fort Morgan, Bon Secour, Lillian, Stapleton and Stockton are unincorporated or census designated places.

Your tax bill shows which levies apply to your address, so read it before you set a price or talk to a buyer. For census purposes the Foley subdivision takes in Gulf Shores, Magnolia Springs and most of Orange Beach, the Daphne subdivision includes Spanish Fort, the Robertsdale subdivision includes Loxley and Silverhill, and the Elberta subdivision includes Perdido Beach.

Storm damage and coastal houses

Tropical weather is a regular fact of life here, and the county has been declared a disaster area several times, with Frederic in September 1979, Ivan in September 2004 and Sally in September 2020 among the named storms. Buyers on the coast look hard at roof condition, wind and flood coverage, drainage and any storm repair left half done.

A house with an open insurance claim or unrepaired damage is a harder sale than a tidy one. If your house is near water, keep your survey and any flood certificate handy. Some owners choose a cash sale to skip repair loans, condition-based appraisals and buyers who walk away after an inspection. We purchase houses as they stand, storm-damaged ones included.

Property tax due dates and penalties

Baldwin has an elected revenue commissioner who serves the whole county. The Collections Division collects tax on all real and personal property assessed in the county. Taxes are due October 1 each year, and courtesy notices usually go out before then so owners can check their mailing address. Collections can be reached at 251-937-0245.

DateWhat it means
October 1Taxes due
December 31Last day before taxes are delinquent
February 28Last day for personal and business checks

After December 31 penalties and interest begin to accrue, and the owner has to contact Collections for the new amount due. Personal and business checks are accepted between October 1 and February 28.

If your mortgage company pays through escrow, confirming the payment is still your job. The county offers an EscrowCheck tool that shows the real-time status of escrow payments from banks and lenders. Search with the parcel number, entered without dashes.

If you cannot find your bill, call the Collections Division before October 1 and ask for a copy. Missing mail does not change the due date, and a late payment adds penalties and interest. Keep proof of payment, such as the receipt or the EscrowCheck result, in the same folder as your closing papers so the title company can see the taxes are current.

How to protest your valuation

The Revenue Commission posts instructions on how to protest an appraised value, whether a protest can be filed by phone, what happens if you miss your hearing and what to do if you never received a valuation notice. A fillable online protest form is available. Answers are collapsed on the county's FAQ page, so open each question for the current instructions.

Do not confuse the valuation notice with your tax bill. The notice states the appraised value and starts the protest clock. The bill arrives later for the October 1 due date.

If you plan to sell, do not let a protest sit. A buyer's title company wants the tax record current, and a pending protest can leave the amount unsettled at closing.

Unpaid taxes and the lien auction

Alabama's 2018 legislature passed Act 2018-577, which gave counties an alternative to selling the property itself: selling the tax lien. Baldwin moved to lien sales in 2019, beginning with tax year 2018 delinquent properties. Every lien for unpaid and delinquent real property taxes is subject to public auction, and the sale runs on the GovEase platform.

The county's tax lien auction page answers the questions an owner would ask: whether ownership transfers when a lien is bought, how to redeem a lien, what happens to liens that do not sell and whether training is available for the platform. Read those answers before you decide anything.

State redemption rules still apply. Our Alabama tax sale page summarizes who can redeem and how long they have.

Selling with taxes owed

The title company pays the delinquent tax, and any lien redemption amount, from your proceeds at closing. Gather three things first: the parcel number, the tax years owed and a payoff figure from Collections.

If the county sold a lien on your parcel, ask Collections what the payoff includes. Request the figure in writing and give the title company time to confirm it. A stale number is the usual cause of a delayed closing.

  1. Call Collections and ask for the payoff for each tax year owed.
  2. Ask whether a lien was sold and who holds it.
  3. Give the written figure to the title company.
  4. Confirm the payment is recorded after closing.

We buy Baldwin County houses as they are, including ones with delinquent tax, storm damage or deferred repairs, so you do not have to fix anything or clear the balance before you accept an offer.

What a cash sale skips is worth spelling out. There is no listing prep, no buyer loan waiting on an appraisal, and no repair negotiation after an inspection. You still need clear paperwork: bring the most recent tax bill, any notice you received from the Revenue Commission, and your mortgage payoff if you have a loan. The title company handles the deed, the payoff of taxes and liens, and the final numbers, and you see them before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

When are Baldwin County property taxes due?

October 1 each year. They become delinquent after December 31, and penalties and interest accrue after that date.

Who collects property tax in Baldwin County?

The Collections Division of the Baldwin County Revenue Commission. You can reach it at 251-937-0245.

What if my mortgage company pays my Baldwin County tax?

Confirm that it did, because that remains the owner's responsibility. The county's EscrowCheck tool shows whether an escrow payment reached the county.

Does Baldwin County sell tax liens or the property itself?

Liens. The county began selling them in 2019 with tax year 2018 delinquents under Act 2018-577, and every lien for unpaid real property taxes goes to public auction.

Can I sell a Baldwin County house with unpaid tax?

Yes, in many cases. The tax and any lien payoff come out of the proceeds at closing, so get a payoff figure from the Collections Division first.

Etowah County housing snapshot

Gadsden, the largest city, is also the seat of Etowah County in northeast Alabama, and the county forms the Gadsden metro area. It held 103,436 people in 2020 and is estimated at 103,886 now, close to 100,000 for decades. The housing count was 47,306 units for 41,974 households, with 11.3 percent of units empty. Homeowners fill 71.1 percent of occupied homes and renters 28.9 percent. Vacancy runs 1.7 percent for owned homes and 10.1 percent for rentals. Urban residents make up 56.8 percent and rural residents 43.2 percent, and the median age is 42.4.

With numbers this steady, most buyers already live nearby. A rental vacancy rate over 10 percent also means a rental house can wait a long time for a tenant. Since 19.9 percent of residents are 65 or older, exemptions for older owners come up often.

The seven cities are Attalla, Boaz (partly in Marshall County), Gadsden, Glencoe (partly in Calhoun County), Hokes Bluff, Rainbow City and Southside (partly in Calhoun County). The towns are Altoona, Reece City, Ridgeville, Sardis City and Walnut Grove. Alabama City is a former city, so older records may use that name, and a very old record from the 1860s may carry the Baine County name, since the county was first created under that name.

School districts

Four districts serve the county: Attalla City, Boaz City, Gadsden City and Etowah County Schools, which covers everything outside the limits of Attalla, Boaz and Gadsden. A house on the line between a city and the county system should be checked against the district map before a listing claims a school.

Due dates and how to pay

The bill is due October 1 and is delinquent on January 1. An unpaid account then runs the calendar below to a sale.

  • October 1: tax due
  • January 1: tax delinquent
  • February: turned over to Probate Court
  • March: Probate Court meets
  • April: advertised for sale
  • May: tax sale

No law makes the Revenue Commissioner mail notices; the mailing is a courtesy, and a missing statement is not an excuse for paying late. Payment options are mail, a visit to the county tax office, or your mortgage company.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Etowah County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Penalties and redemption

Interest and penalty run at 12 percent a year on past due taxes, and property is sold yearly for unpaid taxes. An owner has 3 years from the sale to redeem by paying the taxes, interest, fees and penalties at the same 12 percent rate.

A person who pays someone else's taxes gains no ownership by doing so. A buyer of a house inherits any unpaid prior years, because taxes follow the property. That is why a title opinion comes before any purchase.

Homestead exemptions

Direct questions about appraised value to the Revenue Commissioner, located in the County Courthouse. Any principal residence qualifies for the regular homestead exemption, whatever the owner's age or income, which removes $4,000 of assessed value from state tax and $2,000 from county tax.

TypeWho qualifiesWhat is exempt
Homestead IIOver 65, blind or totally disabled, taxable income of $7,500 to $12,000State tax and $5,000 of county tax
Homestead IIISame group, taxable income below $7,500All property tax
Homestead IVSame group, income above $12,000County tax up to $2,000

The window to apply runs from October 1 to the third Monday in January, though a regular homestead can be claimed any time of year. Types II, III and IV require a signed filing, with tax returns, every year. Nothing is applied for you, so file the claim with the Revenue Commissioner.

Assessment ratios

Alabama sets four classes. Utilities are assessed at 30 percent, all other property at 20 percent, farm, forest and owner-occupied property at 10 percent, and motor vehicles at 15 percent. An owner-occupant therefore pays on a smaller share of value than a landlord does, which matters if a buyer plans to rent the house out.

Buying and selling at the courthouse

Once a sale closes, the buyer files the deed with the Probate Office and takes it to the Revenue Commissioner's office to have the property assessed. A buyer should get a title opinion beforehand, since delinquent taxes follow the property. Alabama Code 40-22-1 sets the recording privilege tax at fifty cents per $500 of value, with the recording fee on top.

A seller can speed things along by cleaning up the tax record early.

  1. Get a payoff for each year owed from the Revenue Commissioner.
  2. Holding a homestead exemption? Tell the office the house is being sold.
  3. Save invoices and permits for storm repairs. An F4 tornado hit the county on Palm Sunday, March 27, 1994, and buyers of older houses ask.
  4. Have the title company confirm the payoff in writing.

Our offers cover Etowah County houses in their current state, including ones with unpaid tax. Whatever is owed comes out of your proceeds at closing.

Preparing to sell in Gadsden and the surrounding towns

Start with the basics a buyer will check. Is the deed in your name, or in the name of someone who has died? Are the tax years paid? Does the house sit in a city, in the county system or on the line between two districts? Answers to those three questions shape almost everything that follows. A short call to the courthouse often settles them in a single morning.

If you rent the house, think about how that affects a sale. A tenant in place may stay or may leave, and a buyer who wants the house empty will price in the wait. A vacant rental carries a full tax bill with nothing coming in, which is why many owners decide to sell rather than hold. Rental vacancy in the county is above 10 percent, so a long wait for a new tenant is realistic.

What a cash sale skips

Most conventional sales depend on a lender. The bank orders an appraisal, an inspector produces a repair list and the closing date drifts as each step wraps up. A cash buyer needs no loan approval. The title search, the tax payoff and the deed recording remain, so begin those first.

Because the offer reflects the house as it stands, nobody asks you to paint, patch or clear out old furniture. A lien or an unpaid tax year is deducted by the title company at closing, and the settlement statement shows the figure before you sign. Weigh that against the time and money a retail listing demands, then choose.

Before the first call, collect the deed, the newest tax statement, any county notice and a line about who occupies the house today. Armed with those, a talk about price and timing is quick.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

If a tax sale is near

The calendar above moves quickly once January arrives. If your house is delinquent and you are weighing a sale, the months between February and May are the tightest. Ask the Revenue Commissioner exactly where your account stands. If the property has already been sold for tax, the 3-year redemption period gives you room, though interest and penalties keep growing at 12 percent a year, so waiting costs money.

An owner in that position can still sell. The title company has to clear the tax sale and the redemption amount from the proceeds, and it will want the paperwork from the sale. Bring every notice you received, even the ones you set aside.

Frequently asked questions

What is the county seat of Etowah County, Alabama?

Gadsden, which is also the largest city. The Revenue Commissioner's office, where assessments are handled, is in the county courthouse.

When are Etowah County property taxes due?

October 1, delinquent January 1, with a tax sale in May.

How much interest applies to late taxes in Etowah County?

Twelve percent a year on past due taxes.

Can I redeem a property sold for taxes in Etowah County?

Yes, within 3 years of the sale, by paying taxes, interest, fees and penalties at 12 percent a year.

Do I get the Etowah County homestead exemption automatically?

No. It has to be claimed with the Revenue Commissioner. The regular homestead can be claimed year round on a principal residence.

Lauderdale County at a glance

Alabama's northwest corner belongs to Lauderdale County. Florence is the seat and the lone city, home to part of the county's 97,135 people (2025 estimate). Of 44,585 housing units, 66.7 percent of the occupied ones are owner-occupied. About half the population is rural, which means a typical seller may hold acreage rather than a city lot.

Water bounds the county on two sides, the Tennessee River to the south and west, with the Elk River and Pickwick Lake adding shoreline. Before listing a low-lying parcel, check its flood exposure. Storm or flood damage is difficult to conceal, and an as-is sale means you can leave repairs undone.

Location also sets the school district: Florence City Schools inside the city, the Lauderdale County School District outside it. Older downtown houses may sit in a historic district with rules on exterior changes, so call the city before planning any work.

Due dates and how to pay

One office, the Lauderdale County Revenue Commissioner, both sets values and takes payment. October 1 is the due date. After December 31 the account is delinquent, with advertising in April and a sale in May for parcels still unpaid.

Way to payDetails
In personCash, check, money order or credit card at the Revenue Commissioner's office
By mailSend payment to the office

With a mortgage escrow, confirm what the lender has already sent so you do not pay twice.

Property classes and the homestead exemption

State law sorts property into three classes. Class I, utilities, is at 30 percent. Class II, other property, is at 20 percent. Class III, which holds farmland, timber and owner-occupied single-family homes, is at 10 percent. Multiply appraised value by the percentage to reach assessed value.

A homestead exemption is for a single-family home that you owned and lived in on the first day of the tax year. Four versions are on offer.

  • H1, the regular exemption: $4,000 of assessed value for state tax and $3,000 for county tax.
  • H2: owners over 65 with adjusted gross income of $12,000 or less.
  • H3: owners who are totally disabled, or over 65 with taxable income under $12,000.
  • H4: owners over 65, whatever their income.

File before December 31. Applying for an over 65 exemption means bringing a driver's license or birth certificate plus your latest federal return. The number for questions is (256) 760-5785.

Taxes when you buy or sell

After buying, an owner has four tasks: put the deed on record in probate court, have the property assessed in their own name at the Revenue Commissioner's office, claim exemptions or current use status, and wrap it all up by December 31 when the purchase predates October 1.

That year's notice will not carry the new owner's name, since the state holds the name and exemptions from the prior October 1. Buyers should therefore verify payment themselves. Owners who add or remove improvements must report that by December 31 as well.

Sellers should make sure the tax line appears on the settlement statement and hold on to the paid receipt. When tax is still owed, the closer requests a payoff from the Revenue Commissioner and takes it from your proceeds. Do this early in the sale. A late payoff request can push the closing date back by days.

Selling a manufactured home

A manufactured home that is not rented or leased has to be assessed at the Revenue Commissioner's office. The county asks for a bill of sale, a title 20 years old or newer and proof that sales tax was paid.

Is there a fee to pay Lauderdale County tax by credit card?

Elmore County housing and growth

East central Alabama holds Elmore County, immediately north of Montgomery and inside that metro area. Wetumpka has the courthouse and Millbrook has the most people. Elmore is one of Alabama's fastest-growing counties. Residents numbered 49,210 in 1990, 65,874 in 2000, 79,303 in 2010 and 87,977 in 2020, and 91,577 are estimated for 2025. In 2020 the county counted 32,567 households and 36,818 housing units, 11.5 percent of them empty. Three quarters of occupied homes, 76.0 percent, are owner-occupied. Homeowner vacancy is 1.5 percent, rental vacancy 6.5 percent, and about 71 percent of the population lives in rural areas.

Your neighbors might be long-time river-town owners or commuters in newer subdivisions. Cities, towns and county lines

The county line cuts through several of these places, and that decides where a deed is recorded and who bills the tax. A parcel in the Autauga part of Prattville or Millbrook belongs to a different county than one in Elmore's part. Look at your tax bill before you contact any office.

The Revenue Commissioner's office

Elmore voters approved a single Revenue Commissioner on March 6, 1990, under Act No. 90-254, and that office combined the jobs of tax assessor and tax collector. It covers about 44,000 parcels across roughly 630 square miles and also values business personal property and personal aircraft.

Visit 100 E. Commerce Street, Suite 102, in Wetumpka, Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., or call 334-567-1184. A Citizen Access Portal and a parcel viewer are linked from the county's website, and both are handy for looking up your own record before you sell.

Alabama Code 40-22-1 sets a recording privilege tax of fifty cents on every $500 of value, with the probate recording fee charged separately. The state treasury takes two-thirds of the tax and the county treasury one-third.

Next, secure the property. Change the locks if keys are unaccounted for, check the roof and the water shut-off, and photograph each room. That record protects you if a question comes up later. Keep the utilities on if you can, since buyers walk through with lights on.

Places and school systems

Athens, home to 25,406 people in 2020, is the biggest city wholly within county lines. Madison and Huntsville extend into it though they belong mostly to Madison County, and Decatur does the same from Morgan County. Ardmore, Elkmont, Lester and Mooresville are towns, while Belle Mina, Capshaw, Tanner, Veto and Greenbrier have no municipal government.

Students are served by five systems: Limestone County Schools across most of the rural area, plus Athens, Decatur, Huntsville and Madison city schools. Bills add up state, county, city and school levies, so an Athens house and a country house are billed differently. Look at the exact parcel instead of assuming a neighbor's bill applies to yours.

Buyers care about access to Interstates 65 and 565 and U.S. 31 and U.S. 72, so name the closest interchange when you describe the house.

  • Low-income owners 65 and older may qualify for broader relief, and an owner who is permanently and totally disabled can qualify at any age.
  • Blind owners can qualify at any age for state-level relief.

An exemption is tied to the resident, not the house. Your buyer will not get yours, and heirs who keep the property must file separately.

How to appeal your assessment

Value disputes go first to the county Board of Equalization. Because the filing window follows the date new values are announced, call the Revenue Commissioner each year for exact dates.

When the board will not change the value, section 40-3-25 points to circuit court. File within 30 days after the board's final decision, notify the board secretary and circuit clerk, and post a bond for costs. A jury request is allowed within 10 days. Whoever loses can go on to the Alabama Supreme Court within 42 days of the circuit judgment.

The prior year's tax must have been paid on time, or bonded, or the appeal cannot go forward. Limestone County makes up the 39th Judicial Circuit.

Start with the parcel number from the portal and your recorded deed. Print the bill and any receipt for the last payment. If anyone besides you holds an interest in the property, such as a co-owner or an heir, learn their names and contact details early, because every one of them may have to sign.

Three situations come up most: inherited houses, rural acreage with an older home, and rentals whose owners are tired of managing them. After an inheritance, list every heir and confirm the deed history. For acreage, learn where your boundaries run and which buildings appear on the record.

Madison County in brief

Up in north central Alabama, Madison County counts 433,516 people in the 2025 estimate, a total beaten only by Jefferson County. Huntsville serves as the seat and is also the biggest city. Redstone Arsenal and the defense and space contractors around it have supplied tens of thousands of jobs, and that steady employment makes house sales here behave differently from those in a typical rural Alabama county.

Housing totals 169,820 units, with 7.1% sitting vacant. Among occupied homes, 66.3% have owners and 33.7% have renters. Since a third of occupied homes are rentals, a tenant is often living in a house when it sells, and that shapes the closing schedule.

The cities are Huntsville, Madison, New Hope and Owens Cross Roads, with Gurley and Triana as towns. Harvest, Hazel Green, Meridianville, Moores Mill and New Market are communities without a municipal government. Whether a city levy lands on your bill depends on the address on your deed. School service is split three ways: Madison County Schools handle the unincorporated areas along with Gurley, New Hope and Owens Cross Roads, Huntsville City Schools cover most of Huntsville, and Madison City Schools also serve Triana.

Due dates and penalties

The due date is October 1 and the delinquency line is December 31. Several details tend to catch new owners off guard.

  • Mailing a bill before delinquency is not a legal requirement. A courtesy notice goes out by October 1, yet if it never reaches you the tax is still late.
  • Whoever owned the parcel on October 1 of the prior year is the name on the bill, so a past owner may keep getting it.
  • Each bill spans the stretch from last October 1 to September 30 of the present year.
  • Once December 31 is behind you, expect a $5.00 late fee, monthly interest of 1% on the base amount, and probate and advertising fees.

After delinquency the account follows the state calendar: probate court in February, advertising in April and sale in May. Lien sales happen only online. Anyone listing a house in winter should check for an unpaid year beforehand, since the payoff climbs every month after January 1.

Tax rates by location

The posted rates are per $100 of assessed value, and a Huntsville address and a rural one are far apart. Resets happen, so ask the collector what is current.

LocationRate per $100 assessed

Madison$6.95

The order of steps is: classification percentage times appraised value gives assessed value, then the rate is applied, and exemptions come off. At equal prices, a house in the city of Madison and one in Huntsville produce noticeably different yearly bills.

How to appeal your assessment

Put your appeal in writing and take it to the Board of Equalization, on the 2nd floor of the Service Center at 1918 Memorial Parkway NW, Huntsville. Code of Alabama sections 40-3-20, 40-3-24 and 40-3-25 govern the process.

Values are reset annually, normally in March or April, and a legal ad runs in the newspaper two weeks in a row. Your 30 days to file begin with the second ad. An appraiser then reaches out to go over the value, and a board hearing follows if the disagreement remains.

If the board rules against you, circuit court is next. Section 40-3-25 gives 30 days from the final decision, and you notify the board secretary and the circuit clerk. Request a jury trial within 10 days of appealing. After the circuit judgment you have 42 days to go on to the Alabama Supreme Court.

One rule trips people up. To keep the circuit appeal alive, pay the taxes by December 31 or post a bond for double the tax due. If you sell mid-appeal, settle that question with your closing attorney first.

Homestead exemptions

The state allows a homestead exemption for a single-family house that is your own primary residence on the tax year's first day, on as many as 160 acres. Applications go to the county office rather than the state.

  • The standard exemption for owners under 65 removes up to $4,000 of assessed value from the state portion and, typically, $2,000 from the county portion.
  • Larger relief is possible at 65 and older, depending on income, under types H-2, H-3 and H-4.
  • A permanent and total disability qualifies an owner at any age, and blind owners get state-level relief.

With the regular exemption, a bill with assessed value of $4,000 or more is reduced by $48 in state and county taxes. After buying, make sure of three things: the deed is on file at the probate office, the Tax Assessor's office has assessed the property, and your exemption has been claimed. A closing attorney often does this, but the responsibility rests with the owner.

Where and how to pay

Payments can be made online, by mail, or at the counter in the Service Center or the satellite office at 100 Plaza Blvd. in Madison. Hours at both are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday to Friday. The main line is 256-532-3370.

  • Card payments cost a 2.75% convenience fee plus $0.30 each, and the county keeps none of it.
  • An e-check costs $1.50.
  • The office no longer takes money orders.
  • For real property in April and May, only certified funds, cash, debit or credit cards work; personal checks are refused.
  • A mailed payment needs a December 31 postmark to dodge the late fee and interest.

Checks are payable to the Madison County Tax Collector. If you hold no bill, email mctaxcoll@madisoncountyal.gov or phone, because the amount due after December 31 moves with fees and interest.

Selling with taxes owed

Closing agents locate any unpaid tax and deduct it from what you receive. Because Alabama bills in arrears, the tax that falls due next October 1 is already building up while the house is yours.

Common snags on Madison County sales include these.

  • An earlier year is unpaid and now carries interest, a late fee and advertising costs.
  • An inherited house whose tax bill still names a deceased parent.
  • A tenant occupies the home and the closing has to fit the lease.
  • The parcel sits on the delinquent list ahead of the May lien sale.

A cash buyer can work around each of these and settle with the county out of the proceeds, so nothing comes from your pocket at the table. Begin by calling the collector for an exact payoff.

October 1 is the date. After December 31 the bill is delinquent and picks up a $5.00 late fee and 1% monthly interest on the base amount.

Where do I file a property value appeal in Madison County?

Go to the Board of Equalization in the Service Center, 1918 Memorial Parkway NW, Huntsville. Thirty days run from the second newspaper advertisement of new values.

Does Madison County mail a tax bill?

Only a courtesy notice is sent, by October 1, and no bill is required before delinquency. Look the parcel up online or call 256-532-3370 if nothing came.

What happens if I do not pay Madison County property tax?

Interest and fees build up, and parcels still unpaid may be offered at the online tax lien sale each May.

Can I sell my Madison County house if taxes are overdue?

Yes. Closing proceeds cover the overdue amount. Get the exact payoff from the collector before picking an asking price.

Marshall County at a glance

Marshall County lies in northeast Alabama on the Tennessee River. Guntersville holds the courthouse seat, while Albertville has the most people. In 2020 the population was 97,612, housing totaled 41,245 units with 9.7% empty, and owners lived in 70.5% of occupied homes. The county appraises roughly 64,000 separate parcels.

Geography drives the bill. Compare a lake-view house near Guntersville with a rural house in the Sand Mountain area and the yearly costs can be far apart. Albertville, Arab, Boaz and Guntersville are the cities, and Cherokee Ridge, Douglas, Grant and Union Grove are towns. Arab, Boaz and the Joppa area partly lie in neighboring counties, and a sliver of Huntsville reaches into Marshall. Find out which county actually bills your parcel.

The total is built from state, county and school district levies, plus a city's in some places. Unincorporated communities such as Asbury, Claysville, Horton and Warrenton are mostly rural parcels. The county keeps two courthouses, one in Guntersville and one in Albertville, so call ahead to learn where your errand is handled.

How the bill is figured

One office handles both valuation and collection: the Revenue Commissioner, found on the courthouse's first floor. It values a house at what it would bring in an open sale to a willing buyer from a willing seller.

Take appraised value, apply the class percentage for assessed value, subtract exemptions, then multiply by the millage rate. One mill equals a tenth of a cent.

October 1 is the due date; December 31 is the last day before delinquency. The state schedule then runs on its own. February sends the delinquent list to probate court, March brings the court's meeting, April is advertising and May is the sale. In other words, a house can land on a sale list roughly five months after it goes delinquent.

Options are mailing the Revenue Commissioner, visiting the courthouse, or letting a mortgage escrow account pay. If a bill is outstanding, request the payoff before you list. The closer needs that number at the table.

Exemptions and current use

Homestead Exemption I is for owner-occupied homes with an owner under 65, and it takes $4,000 off the state tax base and $2,000 off the county base.

Exemption II reaches owners over 65, blind owners and totally disabled owners with adjusted gross income below $12,000 a year, wiping out state tax and county tax on up to $5,000 of assessed value. A third exemption is available to owners over 65 or blind or totally disabled.

Class III land may also qualify for current use valuation, which taxes it on what it is worth to the owner and disregards development potential. Anyone inheriting a house with acreage should ask whether current use is already in place before selling.

How to appeal your assessment

Disputes over value start at the county Board of Equalization. To contest the board's ruling, file within 30 days after its final decision. Under Alabama Code 40-3-25 the board secretary and the circuit court clerk must be notified and a bond posted.

Prior-year taxes must be paid before they go delinquent, or the appeal may be dismissed, unless a supersedeas bond covers it. People overlook this. Keep paying the bill during an appeal, even if you intend to sell.

Before filing, call the Revenue Commissioner. Every parcel has a property record card listing land and buildings, and comparing yours with what stands on the lot can reveal errors.

The tax goes with the owner. A buyer should pay by December 31 even if the bill shows the seller, then verify that the deed was recorded at the probate office and have the property assessed under the buyer's own name.

For an inherited house, find out who is named on the deed and whether the estate has been opened, because that decides who can sign. If tenants live in the house, gather the lease. A buyer will ask for it early, and so will the closer.

Then request a written payoff, share it with the closer, and compare it with the tax line on the draft settlement statement. The two should match.

Allow time for the courthouse. With two locations, Guntersville and Albertville, a trip to the wrong one costs a morning. A short call to confirm the office, the hours and what to bring keeps the sale on schedule. If you live out of the area, ask whether the office can handle the request by phone or mail, and keep a written note of whatever answer you get.

Bring a photo ID and your parcel number whenever you go. If someone else is handling the sale for you, such as an executor, bring proof of that role as well.

Common situations for Marshall County sellers

Inherited houses and homes needing work are the usual cases. Renters live in 29.5% of occupied homes, so some owners are selling a rental with the tenant still there.

Heirs have a distinct problem. An estate can take a year to open, and meanwhile tax notices keep coming in the late owner's name. Missing December 31 starts interest and the probate court timetable.

Payment is due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. You can pay at the courthouse, by mail or through mortgage escrow.

Contact the Revenue Commissioner downstairs at the courthouse. Valuations, new-owner assessments and exemption questions all go through that office.

Yes. Closing normally pays the balance out of your proceeds. Get a payoff number from the Revenue Commissioner before accepting an offer.

A local official has to hear from you first, because the homestead exemption is never applied automatically. Ask the office which forms it needs and whether you must bring proof of age or disability.

If you are selling and already hold the exemption, tell the office the house is changing hands. The buyer cannot rely on yours and will have to file a claim of their own. Timing a sale near the October 1 due date also deserves thought: agree with the buyer in the contract who pays that year's bill, and let the title company prorate it so each side covers its own months of ownership.

Recording a deed

Recording a deed triggers a state tax of 50 cents per $500 of value, rounded up for a partial block, under section 40-22-1. The state treasury keeps two-thirds and the county keeps one-third. A separate probate recording fee applies, and the deed must come with proof of the real sales price on the state's form.

Have your closing agent total all the recording costs before closing day, so the settlement statement holds no surprises.

Selling with taxes owed or repairs needed

We look at Chilton County houses in any condition, including those with unpaid taxes or deferred repairs, and we do not ask you to fix anything first. Selling for cash avoids the lender's appraisal and the repair haggling that so often follows an inspection.

  1. Ask the Revenue Commissioner's office for the balance, listed year by year.
  2. Collect the deed and, if the house was inherited, the probate papers.
  3. Walk the property and jot down anything that differs from the tax record, such as a removed outbuilding or an added room.
  4. Go over the figures with us and decide whether an offer suits you.

Back taxes usually come out of the sale proceeds at closing. Your title company verifies the payoff figure, files the deed and pays you the balance.

What happens at the closing table

Once you accept an offer, a title company or attorney takes over the paperwork. It searches the title, asks the Revenue Commissioner's office for a current payoff, contacts any mortgage holder and prepares a settlement statement that lists every deduction. Read that statement before you sign. Taxes, any mortgage balance and recording costs come off the top, and you receive the remainder.

Sellers of inherited Chilton County property should bring a few extra items: the death certificate if the deed names someone who has died, any probate order and identification for each heir who will sign. Missing one of these can stop a closing. When a house has been vacant, also bring keys, garage openers and a note on the utilities so the transfer is smooth.

Rural parcels deserve one more check. Walk the boundaries or look at a survey if you have one, and tell the title company about any shared driveway, well or easement. These details affect what the deed says and are easy to settle early. They are hard to untangle in the last days before closing, when everyone wants to finish.

Pricing a Chilton County house realistically

Buyers here compare your house with what is for sale in Clanton, Jemison and the rural stretches around them, and a farm-style lot is judged differently from a subdivision lot. Gather a few recent sales close to your address before you accept any number, ours included. Note the age of the roof, the heating and cooling equipment and the septic or well if there is one, because each can move an offer by a real amount.

If the numbers do not work for you, you can say no. We would rather you decide with the full tax picture in hand than feel rushed. Bring any questions about the delinquency calendar to the first conversation, and we will explain how it would apply to your parcel.

What is the county seat of Chilton County, Alabama?

Clanton is the county seat and the largest city. The seat moved there in 1871 after the Grantville courthouse burned.

Is Chilton County rural?

Yes. The 2020 census counted 85.5 percent of residents as living in rural areas and 14.5 percent in urban areas.

When do Chilton County taxes become delinquent?

They become delinquent after December 31, having come due on October 1. The tax sale follows in May.

Do I have to report changes to my house in Chilton County?

Yes, for improvements or removals made on or before October 1. Visit the Revenue Commissioner's office by December 31 to sign a new assessment. Re-roofing, minor repairs and painting do not count.

Can you buy a Chilton County house that needs work or has unpaid taxes?

Yes. We look at houses in any condition, and we can review the tax account together before you decide whether to accept an offer.

Homeowners account for 69.1 percent of occupied homes and renters 30.9 percent, while rental vacancy is 7.7 percent. City dwellers make up 59.7 percent of the population and rural residents 40.3 percent. Nearly 19.9 percent are 65 or older, so senior homestead rules matter a great deal in this county.

The county has four public school systems: Colbert County Schools, Muscle Shoals City, Sheffield City and Tuscumbia City. Which one applies depends on the address, so buyers should verify it. Terrain climbs from river bottom to ridge, putting one house near a floodplain and the next on a slope. If you live by the river or the rail corridor, be ready for questions about noise and flood status.

Homestead exemption

In Alabama a homestead means a single-family, owner-occupied dwelling with up to 160 acres of land. You qualify by owning the house and making it your primary residence as of the first day of the tax year in question.

How a tax bill is calculated

One mill equals a tenth of a cent. The bill comes from multiplying assessed value by the millage rate, and assessed value is a set percentage of appraised value. Your parcel's county, city and school district each contribute to the rate, so equal houses can carry unequal bills.

Two things push a bill up: a vote or board decision to raise the millage rate, or a higher appraised value on the property.

Taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. If no statement reaches you, the obligation is the same. Call the tax office if you move or inherit a house, so statements go to an address you actually check.

All other deeds pay 50 cents per $500 of value, with proof of the real price or value handed to the recorder. If none arrives, the office uses the latest assessment. A person who deliberately holds back proof after being asked faces a penalty of $100 or 25 percent of the tax, whichever is larger.

Compare the name on your deed with your identification. Confirm that the mailing address on file with the county is one you read. Ask whether an exemption is attached to the parcel and who must close it out.

If the property was in a family for generations, add one more step. Old deeds near the eastern county line may carry an outdated boundary reference, because the line moved to Town Creek in 1890. Mention that to the title company so it can check the legal description. A short call now costs far less than a delay on closing day, and it lets you see what is owed before an offer is on the table.

One more habit helps. Photograph the house inside and out before you hand over keys, and keep the pictures with your closing papers. If a question ever comes up about the condition you left it in, you will have a dated record. Plan for these items on closing day: a photo ID, the keys and openers, and any documents the title company requested. If you hold a homestead exemption or an owner's exemption on a manufactured home, mention it at the table so the paperwork reflects the change in ownership and the county knows to stop applying it. County overview

West-central Alabama holds Tuscaloosa County, which stretches across 1,351 square miles. Wooded hills yield to flatter coastal plain as you head south. The Black Warrior River runs through it, and Lake Tuscaloosa spreads over about 5,000 acres. Part of the Talladega National Forest lies inside the line. The city of Tuscaloosa is both seat and biggest city, with Northport and Brookwood rounding out the three. Towns include Coaling, Coker, Lake View, Moundville, Vance and Woodstock.

Population and housing

Bryant, Central and Northridge high schools, and the Tuscaloosa County School System serves everyone outside it. Confirm which one covers your address before you promise a buyer a school zone in the listing. Reasons a value gets reviewed include a building permit, a septic permit, a recent sale or a request from the owner. Because permits can set off a review, a permitted remodel may bring a new valuation, so weigh that before putting money into a house you plan to sell. Ask the assessor's office whether the work you have in mind is likely to change the record.

Mortgage escrow accounts are paid by the lender, and notices for them go out electronically around mid-November. If you pay your own tax, treat the last days of December as a hard stop and send payment early. A postmark of the final day is accepted, but waiting adds risk for no gain.

A tidy file helps the title company, answers the questions a buyer's lender will ask, and shortens the time between acceptance and closing.

  • Estate houses where heirs live outside the county.

The county advertises it online in April and holds the annual sale, online only, in the last week of April.

Calhoun County housing snapshot

Anniston is the county seat of Calhoun County and Oxford is its biggest city; together they make up the Anniston-Oxford metro area in east central Alabama. The 2020 census counted 116,441 residents, and the 2025 estimate of 115,834 shows almost no change. With a steady population, the people who buy your house will mostly be locals.

The 2020 housing count shows 46,437 households sharing 53,052 units, with 12.5 percent of units empty. Homeowners fill 68.4 percent of the occupied homes. Rental vacancy runs 12.2 percent, so a rental house can stay empty for months. An inherited or tenant-worn rental feels that pinch before an owner-occupied family home does. Rural living is common too, since 36.5 percent of residents are outside urban areas.

Watch the county lines. Glencoe and Southside lie partly in Etowah County, Oxford reaches into Talladega and Cleburne counties, and Piedmont reaches into Cherokee County. An Oxford or Glencoe mailing address can therefore belong to a different county's tax rolls than you would guess, and the parcel record settles it. School districts are split by city instead of by county: Anniston City, Calhoun County, Jacksonville City, Oxford City and Piedmont City.

Due dates and delinquent taxes

Bills come due October 1, and any balance left after December 31 is delinquent. The state calendar then runs on its own: the probate court receives the account in February, meets in March, advertises in April and holds the tax sale in May.

The Revenue Commissioner mails statements as a favor, not an obligation, and a lost bill cancels nothing. Houses that sat vacant through an estate or after a tenant moved out are the ones most likely to slide into this calendar unnoticed.

Changes to the property can shift the assessment. Built a deck or a garage? Expect the value to move, and tell the commissioner's office about additions when it asks.

How to appeal your assessment

Your first move is a written protest sent to the county Board of Equalization, due 30 days after your valuation notice arrives. Code of Alabama sections 40-3-20, 40-3-24 and 40-3-25 govern the process.

StepDeadline

Going to court under section 40-3-25 means giving notice to the board secretary and the circuit court clerk and posting a bond the clerk approves. Pay the taxes due, figured on last year's assessment, before they turn delinquent. If you skip that, the court may dismiss your appeal unless you put up a supersedeas bond. Filing an appeal never halts collection, so anyone who appeals and sells in the same year should plan to cover the bill from the sale proceeds.

Online services and the commission office

The county website takes property tax payments online by check or credit card. It also hosts a GIS map with appraisal details searchable by owner or address, and a portal for business personal property. Boat and manufactured home decals and business licenses can be renewed there. Manufactured home renewals run in October and November.

Use the GIS map to look up your own parcel before you talk to a buyer, since it shows what the county has on record. Paying online is handy if closing is near and one bill is still open.

The commission meets in the Ken Joiner Administration Building at 1702 Noble Street in Anniston. The Revenue Commissioner has a tab of its own on the county site, which is the right place to begin with assessing questions.

Recording tax when a house sells

Section 40-22-1 sets the deed tax at 50 cents for every $500 of value conveyed, and a leftover fraction counts as a whole unit. The probate office, which accepts the deed and collects the tax, adds a separate recording fee.

Value already covered by a mortgage on which the mortgage tax was paid is left out, so the final tax can come in under the simple math. Each deed must also carry proof of the actual price, using a Department of Revenue form that the signer attests to. Have your title company calculate the number ahead of closing so it appears on the settlement statement.

Selling a hard-to-sell house

Three situations cause most of the grief: a house needing repairs, an estate with several heirs and a rental left empty. Conventional listings lean on an appraisal, a lender and a patient buyer, and each situation strains at least one of them.

A sensible order of work looks like this.

  1. Look up the parcel and note which county sends the bill.
  2. Find out if the current year is paid and if any earlier year is still open.
  3. Round up the deed, the newest tax statement and probate papers when heirs are involved.
  4. Have the title company quote a payoff for each open year.

Selling for cash removes the lender and the appraisal from the picture. We purchase Calhoun County houses in any condition and can talk through unpaid tax on our first call. Whatever is owed is typically settled from your proceeds at the closing table, so there is nothing to scrape together beforehand.

Heirs need special attention. Where several people share a house, each usually has to sign, and the title company asks for proof of who inherited. Begin that paperwork at once, because tracking down a distant relative or a missing record is what drags a sale out. If the tax is already delinquent, tell every heir at the outset.

What to ask the county before you sell

A short phone call can save a closing. Reach the Revenue Commissioner's office and ask four plain questions. Which tax years show as owed on this parcel? Has any addition or removal been reported that could change the value? Is a protest pending? What name and mailing address does the county hold for the owner? A mismatch in that last answer is common after a death or a divorce, and it explains why bills sometimes go astray.

Keep the replies in one folder together with your deed. If the house is a rental, add the lease status and a note on whether anyone is living there. A buyer who sees a clear paper trail can move faster, and so can you. Anniston is where you will go in person, so allow time for parking and a wait at the counter, and bring photo identification in case staff need to confirm who you are.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Calhoun County property tax due dates?

Taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. The tax sale follows in May after the probate court steps in February, March and April.

How long do I have to appeal my Calhoun County assessment?

You have 30 days from the written valuation notice to protest to the Board of Equalization. After a final board decision, a circuit court appeal must be taken within another 30 days.

Do I owe property tax if I never got a bill in Calhoun County?

Yes. Revenue Commissioners mail notices only as a courtesy, and the tax is owed whether or not a statement arrives.

Why might my Oxford or Glencoe house be taxed by another county?

Several Calhoun County cities cross a county line. Oxford is partly in Talladega and Cleburne counties and Glencoe is partly in Etowah County, so check the parcel record.

Can I sell a Calhoun County house that still has taxes due?

Yes, in many cases. Open taxes are normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Call us with the parcel number and we will look at what is owed before talking about an offer.

Tallapoosa County lies in the Piedmont of east-central Alabama. Dadeville is the seat and Alexander City the largest city. File a written protest with the County Board of Equalization within 30 days of the written notice of valuation. State law sets that window in Code of Alabama sections 40-3-20, 40-3-24 and 40-3-25. The county sets its own hearing dates and forms, so call the office.

Believe the number is inflated? Show up with an appraisal, contractor bids or sales of similar houses nearby. Dated photos of a sagging porch or a bad roof carry more weight than opinions. Keep a copy of everything you hand over, and note the date you mailed or delivered it.

The 2011 tornado on April 27 of that year left repairs behind in parts of the county. Expect an inspector to ask about storm repair history on older houses.

Cities, towns and what the lines mean for a sale

There are four cities: Arab (mostly in Marshall County), Cullman, Good Hope and Hanceville. The nine towns are Baileyton, Berlin, Colony, Dodge City, Fairview, Garden City (partly in Blount County), Holly Pond, South Vinemont and West Point. Many sellers live in one of those communities and not in a city. Confirm which taxing bodies and which school system apply to your parcel before you talk price.

Annual reappraisal

Alabama counties work through one quarter of their parcels annually, which means a full pass takes four years. Buildings discovered in a review go on the rolls for the following tax year. Report new improvements or removals by December 31. A new roof, small repairs and fresh paint do not call for a new assessment. Before selling, make sure a demolished shed or a finished room is reflected correctly, because a mismatch can turn up during a buyer's title work.

When you accept an offer, the title company or attorney starts a search on the parcel, requests payoffs from the Revenue Commissioner's office and from any lender, and writes up a settlement statement. If you have a homestead or age-based exemption, notify the office after closing. The buyer cannot count on yours and will need to apply separately. Keep your closing papers and the final tax receipt in one place, since you may need them when you file your own income taxes for the year of the sale.

Questions a buyer will ask

Which school system serves it? Is the lot on a county road that gets maintained? Answer these before anyone asks and the conversation moves quickly.

Where Talladega County sits

Talladega County occupies east-central Alabama. The city of Talladega is both seat and largest city. The 2020 count was 82,149 people and 37,948 housing units, with 12.8 percent of the units empty. Population has hardly moved: 82,291 in 2010, 82,149 in 2020 and an estimated 81,603 for 2025. Cities, towns and school areas

The five cities are Childersburg, Lincoln, Oxford (partly in Calhoun County), Sylacauga and Talladega. The towns are Bon Air, Munford, Oak Grove, Talladega Springs, Vincent and Waldo. Talladega County Schools is the district named for the county.

Who sends the bill and how to pay

The Talladega County Revenue Commissioner's office collects property tax. Taxes are due every year on October 1 and turn delinquent after December 31.

  • The office takes no payments by phone.
  • Visa, Mastercard and Discover work, with a convenience fee on every card payment.

How the bill is calculated

The county's formula runs in three steps: find the assessed value, multiply by the millage rate, then subtract exemptions. Assessed value is the appraised value times a class percentage.

Class percentages are 30 percent for utility property, 20 percent for commercial, rental, industrial and other non-homestead property, and 10 percent for agricultural, forest and owner-occupied residential property. So a rental is assessed at twice the ratio applied to an owner's own home, and an investor selling a rental should expect a higher bill per dollar of value.

Gather recent comparable sales, repair estimates or an appraisal before you file, since those are the facts a board can weigh.

  • Rentals that went vacant, in a county with a 9.2 percent rental vacancy rate.
  • Houses with deferred repairs that may not satisfy a lender's appraisal.

Once you accept an offer, the title company opens a file and searches the record for liens and unpaid tax. Any Talladega County balance shows up there. The closing agent asks the revenue office for a figure and subtracts it from what you receive. Then you sign the deed, and it is recorded.

Sellers who want fewer surprises can do the groundwork first. Look at your last statement to see whether the house was billed as owner-occupied or as other property, since the class percentage differs. Confirm the mailing address on file. If a relative handled the bills, ask for the paper trail, because a lost notice does not cancel the debt.

With a cash buyer the same checks happen, but no lender sits in the middle. That removes the appraisal wait and the risk of a buyer's loan falling apart over a house that needs work.

A short folder saves days later. Put in it the deed, your most recent tax statement, any letters from the Board of Equalization, receipts for roof, plumbing or electrical work, and a list of every person whose name is on the title. For an inherited house, add the death certificate and any court papers that show who may sell.

If the house sits on acreage, locate the survey. Buyers of rural land in Talladega County often want to see boundaries before they commit, and a missing survey can stall a closing for weeks.

Getting around

Interstate 20 crosses the county, and U.S. Highways 78, 231 and 280 carry the other main traffic. In a listing, name the nearest highway and town. Freight rail runs through as well, which some buyers want to know about.

At a Revenue Commissioner location, by mail to P.O. Box 1119, Talladega, AL 35161, or online. Phone payments are not taken, and card payments carry a convenience fee.

Yes. Non-homestead property such as rentals is assessed at 20 percent of appraised value, while owner-occupied residential property is assessed at 10 percent.

The tax bill stacks county, city and school district levies, so where the house sits matters. An Auburn address and a rural address at the same price can cost quite different amounts each year to hold.

Lee County has four public school districts: Auburn City Schools, Lee County Schools, Opelika City Schools and Phenix City Public Schools. Homestead exemption

To qualify for the state homestead exemption, the property must be a single-family home, your primary residence, owned and occupied by you on the tax year's first day, on no more than 160 acres. Filing is done at the county office.

  • H-1 is for owners under 65 who are not disabled: $4,000 of assessed value off state tax and $2,000 off county tax.

  • H-3 covers owners 65 or older with net taxable income of $12,000 or less on a joint federal return, or those totally disabled, and exempts them from all ad valorem taxes.

If you believe the assessed value is too high, the county Board of Equalization is the first stop. Filing windows come from state law and track the announcement of new values, so ask the county for the current dates.

Last year's taxes must have been paid before delinquency, or covered by a supersedeas bond for twice the tax. Without that the court must throw out the appeal, and it has no power to halt collection of tax already due.

If the tax is not paid

Parcels that stay delinquent are offered at the yearly May tax sale. Redemption is still possible afterward: the owner, heirs, a mortgagee or another interested party has three years from the sale date, and a recorded lienholder is given extra time following written notice.

Under section 40-10-120, a minor or someone under a legal disability may redeem up to one year after the disability ends. A redemption does not by itself restore clean title, so a house with a tax sale in its recent past needs a careful title review before any closing.

Paying off a delinquent balance ahead of May sidesteps all of this. When the sale has already taken place, the redemption clock is ticking and the Revenue Commissioner supplies payoff numbers.

  • Long-held student rentals can carry worn systems and tenants on staggered leases.
  • Inherited houses may have unpaid tax years and several heirs to coordinate.
  • Owners who live elsewhere struggle to oversee repairs and showings.

Questions to settle before you list

Three answers shape your timeline. First, is any tax owed for this year or earlier? Second, does a tax sale appear anywhere in the parcel history? Third, who has the legal authority to sign, especially for an inherited house?

Ask the Revenue Commissioner about the first two and a title company about the third. If the house has tenants, add a fourth: when does the lease end, and will the tenants allow showings? A clear set of answers lets a buyer give you a firm offer and a firm date.

Keep every document in one place: the deed, the tax receipts, any exemption filing and notes from your calls. If something needs correcting, the sooner you find it, the less it costs in time.

What happens at closing

A title company runs a search on the record, finds anything owed and drafts the settlement statement. Tax still due is deducted from what you receive, and the Revenue Commissioner will quote a payoff when asked. With tenants in place, hand over the lease so the buyer can see when it ends.

Have your deed and latest tax receipt on hand. No lender is involved in a cash purchase, so no appraisal or repair haggling slows things down, and you largely pick the closing date. That is a real help when tenants, probate or a move are driving your schedule.

Delinquency starts January 1, advertising follows in April, and the sale itself comes in May.

In general you have three years from the sale date, per Code of Alabama section 40-10-120. Some lienholders and people under a legal disability get more time.

Due dates and penalties

One bill arrives each year, due October 1. Pay after December 31 and it counts as delinquent. A bill left alone moves through the schedule below.

MonthStage of an unpaid bill
October 1Bill comes due
January 1Bill is late

How to appeal your assessment

The county Board of Equalization decides assessment appeals. You have thirty days, counted from the date printed on the notice rather than the day it arrived, and filing is free.

  • Attach evidence. Closing statements, appraisals, comparable sales and insurance values are the examples the county gives.
  • Ask for an informal review before the deadline. The county recommends it, and it can settle a simple error without a formal hearing.
  • An out-of-state agent can file for you, and you do not need a lawyer, provided the agent brings a signed authorization.

The sales used as comparisons come from a fixed period tied to your tax year, and your notice names the dates. Homestead exemption

To qualify for the state exemption, the home must be a single-family house that you own and occupy as your primary residence on the first day of the tax year, on no more than 160 acres. Apply at your county office.

  • Under 65 and not disabled: up to $4,000 of assessed value.
  • 65 or older: the state portion has no maximum.
  • Permanently and totally disabled: the state portion has no maximum.
  • Blind: the state portion has no maximum.

County exemptions run separately and come with income tests. A retiree should ask the county office which kind fits. The exemption follows the owner, so it ends when you sell and the buyer must file a fresh application. Expect the first bill after a sale to look higher for that reason.

What closing looks like at the courthouse

Filing the deed happens at the judge of probate's office. Alabama attaches a recordation tax, 50 cents for every $500 of value conveyed. Closing agents file the paperwork on your behalf, so you seldom visit the recording desk yourself. Selling with taxes owed

  3. Instruct the title company to pay the tax balance from your proceeds, and ask for a line showing it on the settlement statement.
  4. Work out who signs: every owner named on the deed, plus a personal representative where an owner has died.
  5. After liens are cleared, the closing agent files the deed with the probate judge.

Nothing. The Board of Equalization charges no filing fee, but the appeal has to arrive within thirty days of the date on your notice.

October 1. They go delinquent after December 31, and unpaid accounts head toward probate court and a tax sale in May.

The Board of Equalization, working with the county Appraisal Department. For real property, write to propertytaxappeals@mc-ala.org or call (334) 832-1327.

Can I sell a Montgomery County house with back taxes owed?

Yes. Get the payoff amount from the county and ask the title company to pay it from your proceeds. A cash buyer can often build that payoff into the deal.

No. An attorney is optional, and an out-of-state agent can file as well if the agent supplies a signed authorization.

Dale County and its housing market

Dale County occupies southeast Alabama's Wiregrass region, roughly forty miles from both Georgia and Florida. Its seat and biggest city is Ozark, and the county makes up the Ozark micropolitan area within the broader Dothan-Ozark region. Because the footprint is small, houses in Ozark, Daleville, Level Plains and the farm towns all answer to one county revenue office and one probate office.

Roughly 49.5 percent of residents live in urban areas.

Old deeds sometimes carry history. The county seat was once Dale's Court House, now Daleville, and later Newton before Ozark took over in 1870, so a parcel description that names one of those places may point to an older title chain. Title companies like a clean search before closing anywhere in the county.

Fort Rucker and military sellers

Most of Fort Rucker lies inside Dale County, and the county commission describes it as the home of Army Aviation and a primary training base for military helicopter pilots. The county site now lists the post as Fort Novosel. Ozark and Daleville each border the installation, and military families come and go on orders.

A seller leaving on orders rarely has months to wait through showings and repairs. A direct cash sale with a short closing date fits that schedule and removes the worry of holding an empty house in another state. Cities, towns and school zoning

The county has five cities and seven towns. The cities are Daleville, Dothan (partly in Houston and Henry counties), Enterprise (partly in Coffee County), Level Plains and Ozark. The towns are Ariton, Clayhatchee, Grimes, Midland City, Napier Field, Newton and Pinckard. Skipperville, Echo, Clopton, Kelly and Rocky Head are unincorporated. A home in an unincorporated place answers mainly to the county, while a city address adds city rules for code enforcement and utilities.

Schools vary by address. The Dale County School District serves most unincorporated areas. Daleville City Schools and Ozark City Schools cover their own cities, and Enterprise City Schools and Dothan City Schools cover the parts of those cities inside the county. Elementary students living on Fort Rucker attend Department of Defense Education Activity schools, and families on the post may choose Daleville, Enterprise or Ozark schools for the secondary grades. Taxes and a sale

Taxes attach to the land and the house, never to a particular owner. Whoever holds title has to clear delinquent tax, including years from before they bought. For that reason the closing agent looks for open balances and subtracts them from what the seller receives.

Homestead status deserves a question at a sale. The regular homestead exemption is for a principal residence and can be claimed year round, so a buyer who moves in should ask the Revenue office how to file for it. If you are the seller, let the office know the house has changed hands.

Recording a deed

Filing a deed triggers the privilege tax in Alabama Code section 40-22-1, which is fifty cents for every $500 of value. Probate staff collect it when the deed is filed, with a separate recording fee, and the proceeds divide two-thirds state, one-third county.

  • A rental the owner can no longer afford to repair, with the tenant gone.
  • A military family that has left on orders while the house sits listed.

Roads matter little here for the paperwork but plenty for buyers. U.S. 84 runs east and west, U.S. 231 runs north and south through the Ozark area, and state routes fill in the rest. The Dale County Revenue office handles assessment and collection locally, and the Probate Office records deeds.

Yes. Alabama taxes follow the property, so unpaid years must be settled by the current owner. The balance is usually paid from sale proceeds at closing.

What is the deed tax on a Dale County sale?
