Russell County and the Georgia line

Russell is Alabama's easternmost county. The Chattahoochee River separates it from Columbus, Georgia, and Phenix City, the county seat and largest city, is part of that two-state metro area. The 2020 census counted 59,183 people, up 11.8% from 52,947 in 2010, and the 2025 estimate eased back to 58,898. Of 27,253 housing units, 11.9% were vacant. Among the 23,997 households, 57.1% owned and 42.9% rented, so a sale with a tenant already living in the house is an everyday event here. About 40% of residents live in rural areas, so many properties sit outside city lines. That mix of renters, commuters and country lots means buyers arrive with very different expectations, and a good description helps each of them see whether your house fits.

The state line shapes daily life. More than 54% of working residents commute to another state, mostly to Columbus. Phenix City unofficially keeps Eastern time although Alabama officially uses Central, which is why the county website tags many events with ET. Whenever you book a closing or an office visit, ask which clock the appointment uses, because a one hour mix-up can cost you the day. U.S. 80 and U.S. 280 run toward Columbus, and U.S. 431 and several state routes also serve the county.

Commuters care about location, so describe it plainly. A house in Hurtsboro or the rural south reads very differently from one a few minutes from the bridges into Georgia, and buyers who work in Columbus will price that difference.

Communities and local features

Phenix City is the lone city, and Hurtsboro is the lone town. Ladonia is a census-designated place, and the unincorporated list is long: Cottonton, Crawford, Fort Mitchell, Glenville, Hatchechubbee, Holy Trinity, Hooks, Jernigan, Mahrt, Pittsview, Sandfort, Seale, Uchee and Wende. Crawford and Seale were once county seats and are now unincorporated communities outside Phenix City.

Schools come from the Russell County School District. Because attendance follows the address, confirm the district for the specific house before you compare it with another. A home near the Chattahoochee River or the Eufaula National Wildlife Refuge, which reaches into the county, deserves a call to the insurer about flood questions before a buyer asks.

Residents have been invited to give input on Comprehensive Plan 2050, a long-range plan for the county. Plans of this kind can steer zoning, roads and utilities for decades, so anyone holding land outside Phenix City may want to follow the meetings and mention the plan to buyers.

Due dates and the tax sale

Property taxes in Alabama come due October 1 and turn delinquent after December 31. The state schedule sends an unpaid parcel through these steps:

  • October 1: taxes due.
  • January 1: delinquent.
  • February: sent to probate court.
  • April: advertised for sale.
  • May: tax sale.

You can visit the courthouse at 1000 Broad Street in Phenix City. Each year the Revenue Commissioner's office posts a notice on the county website with the tax sale date and the registration time. Details shift from year to year, so read the current notice rather than trusting an old date. Sellers should ask for a payoff figure early. Once a parcel has been advertised, the days left are few, and a payoff request takes a little time to answer.

Homestead exemption

To get the exemption, the house must be a single-family home you own and live in as your main residence on the first day of the tax year, with no more than 160 acres. Apply at the county office, and the amount shrinks your taxable value.

Owner situationWhat is exempt
Under 65Up to $4,000 of assessed value off the state tax and up to $2,000 off the county tax
65 or older, income at or under $12,000 on the combined federal returnAll ad valorem taxes (type H-3)
Permanently and totally disabledAll ad valorem taxes, no income limit (also H-3)
65 or older, higher incomeState portion, plus the regular $2,000 county exemption (H-4)

Because the exemption travels with the owner rather than the property, a buyer has to file their own application. Their first bill may therefore run higher than yours did.

What the deed tax costs

Alabama Code 40-22-1 sets the deed tax at 50 cents for every $500 of value. The probate judge's office takes payment at the moment of recording, then sends a third to the county treasury and the other two thirds to the state. Staff expect proof of the price actually paid. A mortgage that already settled its own tax lowers the amount that counts. Deeds made for nominal consideration to fix a title defect are excluded.

The closing agent normally works out the amount and shows it on the settlement statement. To see the number ahead of time, ask the agent for an estimate before you accept any offer. Deeds that only correct a title defect, with no real price, are handled differently, so mention that purpose if it applies to your paperwork.

Steps to sell a Russell County house

A sale here follows the same path whether a buyer uses a loan or pays cash. It helps to see the order before you start.

  1. Collect the deed, your newest tax bill and a payoff letter from any lender.
  2. Phone the Revenue Commissioner's office to learn what the parcel owes, delinquent amounts included.
  3. If an owner has died, find out who can legally sign for the estate.
  4. Pick a closing agent to search the title, clear liens and prepare the settlement statement.
  5. Proceeds cover the tax balance and any liens. After that, the deed is recorded with the probate judge in Phenix City.

Owners who now live out of state, heirs especially, can often sign by mail or in front of a notary where they live. Tell the closing agent as early as you can so the paperwork is routed in time.

What Russell County sellers face

Sellers here often own a house inherited from family, a rental with tenants or a property where repairs have piled up. The Columbus commute market is steady, but older houses still need money to list well.

Cash Home Buyers reviews Russell County houses as they stand, from Phenix City neighborhoods to Seale, Crawford and Hurtsboro, and replies with a written offer. A cash closing can skip appraisals tied to a buyer's loan, and you can ask about timing that fits a tax deadline or a move. With a tenant in place, bring the lease and deposit records. With an heir involved, bring the estate papers. Whatever the situation, weigh the offer against what a listing would net after repairs and months of showings, then pick the route that fits your calendar. Ask the buyer to put the closing date and the list of who pays which costs in writing.

Frequently asked questions

What county is Phenix City, AL in?

Russell County, where it serves as the county seat. A small piece of the city extends into Lee County.

When are Russell County property taxes due?

Bills are payable from October 1 and delinquent once December 31 passes. A parcel left unpaid follows the state schedule toward a sale in May.

How much is the deed tax in Russell County?

Fifty cents per $500 of value, set by Alabama Code 40-22-1. It is paid to the probate judge's office when the deed is filed.

Does Russell County use Eastern or Central time?

Alabama is officially on Central time, but Phenix City unofficially uses Eastern time. Confirm the time zone when you schedule an appointment or a closing.

Can I get a homestead exemption in Russell County?

Yes, if you live there as your main home on the first day of the tax year. File at the county office. What you receive depends on age, disability and income.

DeKalb County at a glance

DeKalb County fills Alabama's northeast corner against the Georgia line. Fort Payne is the seat and the largest city, and the other two cities are Henagar and Rainsville. Seventeen towns round out the list: Collinsville (partly in Cherokee County), Crossville, Fyffe, Geraldine, Hammondville, Ider, Kilpatrick, Lakeview, Mentone, Pine Ridge, Powell, Sand Rock, Shiloh, Sylvania and Valley Head. Sulphur Springs, Grove Oak, Dawson and Whiton are unincorporated. Plenty of residents commute to jobs in nearby counties.

Residents numbered 71,608 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 74,085 marks a 3.5 percent gain. There were 30,584 housing units and 27,145 households, with 11.2 percent of the units vacant. Owners hold 74.0 percent of occupied homes and renters 26.0 percent. About 88.3 percent of residents live in rural areas, so many houses sit on acreage and not on city lots. An empty house still carries a full tax bill each October.

A seller in a small town may deal with different utilities and code officers than one in Fort Payne, so make the town hall your first call.

Weather and structural history

Buyers look closely at older mountain houses, and the county has had events that explain why. An earthquake of magnitude 4.6 on April 29, 2003, centered near the county's eastern edge, cracked foundations and brought down a chimney. The April 27, 2011 Super Outbreak included the Rainsville tornado, rated EF5.

A house with older storm repairs, a cracked foundation or a patched roof can still sell, though it often takes a buyer willing to skip a long repair negotiation. Keep receipts and permits for repairs, and say plainly what was fixed and when. Problems that come out in an inspection hurt the price more than problems you disclosed first.

How Alabama classifies property for tax

Alabama sets assessment ratios by class, and the ratio decides what share of market value is taxed. The four classes apply statewide.

ClassType of propertyAssessment ratio
IUtilities30%
IIAll other property20%
IIIFarm, forest and owner-occupied10%
IVMotor vehicles15%

An owner-occupied house in DeKalb County falls in Class III at the lower ratio. A rental house falls in Class II, so a landlord's bill on the same market value runs higher. If you rent out a house you are selling, expect the buyer's tax picture to differ from yours.

Due dates and the delinquency timetable

October 1 is the due date, and a balance open past December 31 goes delinquent. From there the state calendar leads to a May tax sale.

  • October 1: due
  • January 1: delinquent
  • February: turned over to Probate Court
  • March: Probate Court meets
  • April: advertised for sale
  • May: tax sale

Phone the county Revenue Commissioner's office in Fort Payne to learn the exact payoff and when the office is open. Do this ahead of choosing a closing date. A written figure lets the title company match its own numbers.

Recording a deed

Putting a deed on record costs a privilege tax of fifty cents per $500 of value, set by Alabama Code section 40-22-1, plus a separate recording fee at the probate office. The county gets one-third of the tax and the state two-thirds.

Either party must disclose the real price on a state revenue form. When no proof of price comes in, the tax may be figured on the latest assessment, and a penalty can follow.

Contesting a high assessment

Disagree with your valuation? The county Board of Equalization hears the challenge first, and circuit court is the next step if you lose. Under section 40-3-25 you have 30 days for that court appeal, and the tax keeps coming due while it is pending. Confirm the current rules with the Revenue Commissioner before you file.

Selling a house with tax problems

Rural acreage and older mountain houses bring their own difficulties.

  • An inherited house on land with several years of unpaid tax.
  • A rental assessed in Class II with a tenant who has left.
  • Storm or foundation damage that makes financing hard for a retail buyer.
  • A property on a private or mountain road that few agents want to show.

Because Alabama taxes follow the property, any unpaid balance usually comes out of the proceeds at closing. A cash buyer will take the house in its current state, settle the back taxes from the sale and close when you are ready.

  1. Request a payoff in writing from the Revenue Commissioner.
  2. Pull together the deed plus probate papers if you inherited.
  3. List road access or easement quirks for the title company.
  4. Weigh the offers and pick a closing date.

A road that is private or steep deserves a mention at the start. Tell any buyer who will do the maintenance and whether a written agreement exists, since lenders often ask.

From first call to closing

Once you decide to sell, the steps are few. We discuss the house, where the taxes stand and what timeline suits you. Should you want an offer, we view the property and quote a figure. Accept it, and a title company opens a file, orders the search and requests payoffs. You sign, funds move, and the deed is recorded at the probate office.

The slowest part is usually paperwork, not price. Names on the deed need to match your identification. Every owner has to sign, so if the house passed to heirs, locate them early. A lien from an old loan or a contractor can appear in the search, and clearing it takes time, so ask the title company to run its search as soon as you have an offer in hand.

At the table, read the settlement statement. Taxes, any mortgage payoff and recording costs come off the top, and you receive the rest. Keep a copy with your tax records.

Land, roads and boundaries

Because so many DeKalb houses are rural, land details can decide a sale. Know your acreage and where the lines run. If you have a survey, find it. If you do not, tell the buyer so, and expect the title company to ask whether a boundary has ever been disputed. A neighbor's fence, a creek or an old logging road can all blur a line.

Interstate 59 and U.S. 11 are the main routes, with state routes linking the smaller towns, and Norfolk Southern also runs through the county. A house near these is easier to reach and to show. One up a mountain road may need a four-wheel-drive visit, and agents often pass on it. That is one reason owners of such houses look at a direct sale.

Part of Little River Canyon National Preserve lies inside the county, and buyers who want land near it tend to ask about trails, water and access. Mention anything you know about springs, wells or septic systems, because rural buyers ask about them first.

Frequently asked questions

What is the county seat of DeKalb County, Alabama?

Fort Payne is the county seat and the largest city.

What is the assessment ratio for a home in DeKalb County?

An owner-occupied home falls in Class III at 10 percent of value. Other property, including most rentals, is Class II at 20 percent.

When do DeKalb County property taxes become delinquent?

After December 31. The January 1 delinquency date is followed by a May tax sale.

How much is the deed recording tax in DeKalb County?

Fifty cents for each $500 of value under Alabama Code 40-22-1, plus the probate recording fee. The state keeps two-thirds and the county one-third.

Can I sell a DeKalb County house that has unpaid taxes?

Yes. The unpaid balance is normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing, because Alabama taxes follow the property.

Two county seats, one set of taxes

Ashville and Pell City both serve as seats of St. Clair County. Mountains at the tail end of the Appalachians cut the county in two, and Pell City was added so the southeast side had a courthouse nearer to home. Government business can land in either town.

Before any trip, phone the Revenue Commissioner and find out which location holds your parcel and whether a visit is required at all. The county website is the other quick check.

Population and housing

St. Clair County lies in central Alabama within the Birmingham metro area, with Pell City as its biggest city. Residents numbered 91,103 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 98,206. Growth has continued at each count since 1980, when the total was 41,205. Of 37,775 housing units, 9.0 percent stood vacant, and 81.2 percent of occupied homes had owners living in them. Roughly 67.1 percent of the population is rural, which means buyers often ask about wells, septic and road access.

Taxes follow the parcel. Whether a house sits inside a city limit and which districts cover it shape the bill far more than the town on the mailing label. Trussville and Leeds are mostly in other counties even though pieces extend here.

Due dates and penalties

The tax year turns on October 1. Pay through December and nothing extra is added. Once January arrives the account moves onto a month-by-month collection schedule.

DateWhat happens
October 1Taxes due
December 31Last day to pay without delinquency; also the deadline to report improvements
January 1Taxes become delinquent
FebruaryUnpaid accounts go to probate court
MarchCourt meets on the delinquent list
AprilDelinquent parcels are advertised
MayTax sale

No law makes the county mail a bill. A courtesy notice usually comes from the Revenue Commissioner, yet one that never arrives wipes out nothing. Own a St. Clair County property you rarely visit? Phone and ask for the balance.

How assessment works

Everything starts from an appraised value. As the state illustrates it, a 10 percent assessment rate turns $100,000 into $10,000 before millage is applied. The bill climbs if millage goes up or if the appraisal rises through reappraisal or a hot market.

Alabama counties examine one quarter of their parcels annually under what is called annual equalization, so any given parcel gets a thorough review every fourth year. The intent is smaller annual changes in place of big four-year leaps.

New construction needs a fresh signed assessment, due by December 31 for work completed by October 1. Additions, pools, remodels, a new bath, a deck, patio, carport or garage all belong on that list. A new roof or a paint job does not.

Homestead exemption

A single-family home on up to 160 acres can qualify when the owner lived there on the first day of the tax year. Owners over 65, permanently and totally disabled owners and blind owners are relieved of the state portion, although county taxes may remain. Apply through the local county office.

About 17.4 percent of county residents were 65 or older in 2020, so the age group covers a lot of owners. Heirs selling a parent's home should learn whether a claim was on file, because the state portion of the bill depends on it. After inheriting from an exempt owner, ask what must be filed in your own name.

Buyer and seller duties at transfer

The new owner records the deed with the probate office, then takes it to the revenue commissioner to be assessed. Bills sometimes keep arriving under the previous owner's name, but the responsibility follows the property.

Three tasks for a seller before the closing date:

  • Find out which year is paid and if anything is still owed.
  • Spell out in the contract who covers the current year.
  • Send any change of address to the county in writing.

Think the value is too high? Get the appeal form and its deadline from the revenue commissioner before you list, so a lender does not stumble over it later.

Selling with taxes owed

An unpaid balance rarely blocks a sale. Begin with a call to the revenue commissioner for this year's amount plus any earlier years, and request the number in writing for the closing agent.

On closing day the title company sends the county its share out of your proceeds, and the deed then goes to probate for recording. Carry the deed or your latest tax statement, a photo ID, and paperwork on any exemption or recent improvement. If bills went to a stale address, give the new one to the county so later notices find you.

A cash purchase leaves these tax steps unchanged. The buyer takes the home as it stands, the county is paid from proceeds, and you skip the weeks spent waiting on a lender's appraisal.

What to expect once you list

Buyers and title companies tend to ask about tax status in the first week, so have answers ready. Gather the last bill, the deed and notes on any building work, because additions and remodels affect what the county should already hold on file.

Say you added a deck, garage or extra bathroom and never reported it. Tell the revenue commissioner now. That is simpler than untangling it at the closing table. Buyer's agents also check whether the parcel is inside a city, since that decides which districts apply.

Rural parcels, common here, bring extra questions on wells, septic and access roads. Round up any permits or inspection records, and decide early between a standard listing, with showings and an appraisal wait, and a direct sale to a cash buyer who accepts the property in its current condition.

From listing to closing

A typical sale moves in a few stages. First comes pricing and photos. Next an offer arrives, and an inspection and title search follow. The title search is where any county tax balance or lien appears, and the closing agent then orders a payoff. Finally the deed is signed and sent to the probate office.

Tax questions tend to surface at the title stage, so settle them early. A parcel with a clear record closes faster. With a cash buyer, several of these stages shrink, because no lender is waiting on an appraisal and a closing date can be set around your schedule.

If you live out of town, a signed power of attorney or a mobile notary can handle the paperwork. Confirm with the title company which documents they accept before you arrange either one.

Roads and landmarks

Interstates 20 and 59 pass through, together with U.S. 11, 78, 231 and 411 and assorted state routes. Logan Martin Lake and Horse Pens 40, a private park on Chandler Mountain, bring visitors and color how lake and mountain properties are advertised. Public schools belong to the St. Clair County School District. In a listing, mention the district and the nearest town.

Frequently asked questions

When are St. Clair County property taxes due?

October 1, with delinquency after December 31. Unpaid bills can move to a probate court tax sale in May.

Why does St. Clair County have two seats?

Ashville and Pell City share the role because mountains divide the county. Pell City was added to serve the southeast.

Do I owe tax if no bill came?

Yes. The revenue commissioner need not mail notices, and the owner is responsible whether a statement arrives or not.

Must I report improvements to my house?

Yes, for additions, new structures, pools, remodeling and similar work done by October 1. Sign a new assessment by December 31. Re-roofing and painting do not need one.

How do I appeal a St. Clair County assessment?

Contact the County Revenue Commissioner's office for the form and the deadline.
